Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 77
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Delivery Driver
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress, Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Doubt: I can't trust that I will do the right thing, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

Vignette:
Arthur, at seventy-seven, had always prided himself on his reliability, a quality that served him well in his long career as a delivery driver. His routes were familiar, his customers accustomed to his steady presence. Life, he believed, was largely predictable, and people, for the most part, were decent. That belief shattered one late autumn evening, barely eight months ago. He had been on his final drop-off in a quiet residential street, the porch light barely illuminating the package in his hand, when two figures emerged from the shadows. The confrontation was swift, brutal, and disorienting. He remembered the jarring impact, the scramble for his keys, and the sickening thud as he hit the pavement, his delivery van disappearing into the night. Left shaken and bruised, the world he thought he knew evaporated around him.

In the weeks and months that followed, Arthur felt a profound shift within himself. The once-familiar streets now held a lurking menace. The simple act of stepping out of his van, especially as dusk approached, would trigger a prickle of dread, his eyes darting to every shadow, every parked car. He found himself constantly scanning, hyper-aware of footsteps behind him or the sudden sound of a car door slamming, his heart quickening with an almost suffocating fear. This pervasive sense of danger fed a deeper, more insidious doubt: *he couldn't trust that he would do the right thing*. He replayed the incident endlessly, questioning if he should have fought harder, run faster, or simply surrendered without resistance. He felt a profound incompetence, a failure to protect himself, and this self-doubt began to seep into other areas of his life, making him second-guess even the simplest decisions on his delivery route.

To manage the churning distress, Arthur developed a relentless routine of busyness. He started taking on extra shifts, volunteering for the longest routes, and meticulously reorganizing his garage in the evenings. He’d meticulously plan his routes, sometimes adding unnecessary detours, anything to keep himself occupied and his mind from wandering. He was certain that *if he thought about the event, he would not be able to handle it*. The memory, he believed, was a dangerous, volatile thing, capable of overwhelming him completely, and so he worked hard at keeping busy with other things, actively pushing away any intrusive images or feelings. If a fragment of the assault surfaced, he would immediately redirect his attention, focusing intently on the road ahead or the next task at hand, suppressing thoughts about the trauma with a fierce determination.

When the agitation became too much to bear, especially after long days on the road, Arthur found solace in food. He started eating excessively, particularly in the evenings, reaching for comfort in large, unthinking portions. It was a temporary reprieve, a way to numb the gnawing anxiety and the constant mental effort of avoidance. His wife, Martha, noticed his increasing withdrawal and the extra weight he was carrying, but her gentle inquiries were met with vague assurances of being "just tired." His relentless schedule meant less time at home, and when he was there, his mind was often elsewhere, consumed by vigilance or the effort of suppression. The job he once loved, the one that gave his later years purpose, had become a minefield of potential triggers, and the continuous effort to avoid them was exhausting him. He felt perpetually on edge, caught in a cycle of fear and avoidance, and the world had become a far more dangerous place than he had ever imagined. It was Martha's growing concern, and his own profound weariness from constantly battling his own mind, that finally brought him to seek help, though he wasn't entirely sure what good it would do. He just knew he couldn't keep going on like this, constantly afraid of what might happen if he stopped being busy, or if he finally allowed himself to think about that night.
